screens.title: SOLID Design: Single Responsibility & Open/Closed
screens.narratorSegment: As your projects grow, fragile classes and rigid conditionals become the main source of bugs and slow change. In this lesson we concentrate on two SOLID rules that help avoid that: Single Responsibility, which keeps classes focused on one reason to change, and Open/Closed, which enables adding features without altering tested code. You will see concrete Java examples that first demonstrate common violations and then show how to refactor them into clearer, testable components. For SRP we use a ReportGenerator that mixes data access, formatting, and output; for OCP we use a discount calculator that uses conditional logic instead of polymorphism. Each example highlights why cohesion and low coupling matter for testing, team work, and incremental extension. By the end you will be able to spot responsibilities that should be separated, design small interfaces, and choose strategy-style abstractions to add new behavior safely. Think about the last time you changed a class and unintentionally broke a feature — this chapter gives you patterns to prevent that. Ready to learn how to turn a Swiss army knife class into a set of precise tools?

screens.narratorSegment: This chapter pairs explanation with practical refactoring. You will refactor a Task class that currently mixes persistence, notification, and business state into separate collaborators. screens.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
screens.narratorSegment: Single Responsibility means a class should have one primary reason to change. Practically, that means its responsibilities should be cohesive: methods and fields should support a single domain of concern. A reason to change is often tied to a stakeholder or a feature area. For example, database schema changes are one reason, formatting requirements another, and notification delivery a third. When these concerns live inside the same class, a small change in one area can break unrelated behavior, and tests become brittle. High cohesion and low coupling are the desired outcomes: cohesion groups related behavior, while low coupling reduces ripple effects between modules. A common mistake is thinking SRP requires a class with only one method; the goal is meaningful grouping, not tiny classes for their own sake. To evaluate a class, ask: who would request a change here? If different teams or features would make separate requests, you likely have an SRP violation. As a concrete example, the ReportGenerator that fetches data, formats it, and prints it mixes three reasons to change. Refactoring splits those into a fetcher, a formatter, and a printer, which improves testability and lets each piece evolve independently. Consider: what single responsibility would you give your next class?

keyIdea.title: SRP
keyIdea.text: Design classes so each has a single, clear reason to change to reduce coupling and make testing easier.

content.html:
Core Concept

Single Responsibility Principle

A class should have one reason to change: group related behavior and separate unrelated concerns.

Why it matters

Improves modularity, makes unit tests focused, and reduces unintended side effects when requirements change.

Misconception

SRP doesn't demand microscopic classes; it asks for a single cohesive responsibility, not a single method.

Check your understanding

List the stakeholders or reasons to change for a class you wrote recently. Do they align or conflict?

Example — Violating SRP
// SRP Violation Example
class ReportGenerator {
    public String fetchData() {
        System.out.println("Fetching report data...");
        return "Raw Data: ...";
    }

    public String formatReport(String rawData) {
        System.out.println("Formatting report...");
        return "Formatted Report: " + rawData.toUpperCase();
    }

    public void printReport(String formattedReport) {
        System.out.println("Printing report: " + formattedReport);
    }

    public void generateAndPrintReport() {
        String data = fetchData();
        String formatted = formatReport(data);
        printReport(formatted);
    }
}
Concrete Example

The class handles data access, presentation formatting, and output. Each would change for different reasons.

Key Takeaway

Split responsibilities into focused collaborators to reduce ripple effects from changes.

screens.title: SRP Violation: ReportGenerator Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the ReportGenerator example to understand exactly why it violates SRP. The class contains methods to fetch data, format it, and print it. Each method corresponds to a different reason to change: if the data source changes, you modify fetching; if the layout or header requirements change, you modify formatting; if output moves to email or file, you alter printing. Mixing these in one class creates high coupling: tests for the formatter may need database setup, and a change to printing could break report content. A concrete run shown in the code prints messages for each step, which is useful for demonstration but not for production. A common misconception is to treat logging or convenience printing as harmless responsibilities — in practice they create hidden dependencies and make code harder to reuse. When you refactor, you extract responsibilities into classes such as ReportDataFetcher, ReportFormatter, and ReportPrinter, each replaceable or mockable in isolation. In the next screen we'll show the refactored version with small, testable classes and describe how cohesion improves and coupling decreases. Ask yourself: which collaborator would you mock in a unit test for formatting?

keyIdea.title: Why it's a problem
keyIdea.text: Mixing data access, formatting, and output in one class couples unrelated change reasons and hinders testing.

content.html:
Definition

SRP Violation: ReportGenerator

We inspect how responsibilities are mixed and why that harms maintenance and tests.

Problems to notice
  • Different stakeholders influence fetching, formatting, and output.
  • Unit tests become integration tests when concerns are combined.
  • Changing one behavior may require touching unrelated code paths.
Common mistake

Keeping convenience methods like printing in business classes because it's simple now, which creates hidden dependence later.

Code Walkthrough
// Usage in main
public class BadReportApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ReportGenerator generator = new ReportGenerator();
        generator.generateAndPrintReport();
    }
}

// Console output shows all steps tied together, which hides separable responsibilities.
Concrete example

If the team replaces the data source with an API, fetchData changes and risks affecting formatting and printing code in the same class.

Key takeaway

Identify the responsibilities and extract collaborators so each can change without cascading edits.

screens.title: SRP Refactor: Split Report Responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring to respect SRP means extracting collaborators with clear roles. In the example refactor we create ReportDataFetcher to handle data retrieval, ReportFormatter to prepare the presentation, and ReportPrinter to handle output. Each class exposes a small A P I: fetch returns raw data, format produces a textual report, and print sends the report to a destination. That separation allows focused unit tests: you can test formatting with mocked raw data, test printing with a fake output sink, and test fetching with an isolated data source or stub. The refactored main function composes these collaborators and performs the workflow. This approach raises cohesion inside each component and lowers coupling between them. A misconception is that this adds too many classes; however, these smaller classes are simpler to reason about, easier to name, and tend to have fewer dependencies. When you refactor, keep behavior unchanged initially and run simple console checks. Later you can replace implementations—swap a console printer for an email sender—without touching the formatter. As you practice, ask: which tests become isolated after extraction, and which integration tests remain? SRP Refactor: Split Report Responsibilities means extract focused collaborators so changes to data, formatting, or output are isolated and testable.. In practical terms, refactoring reportgenerator into fetcher, formatter, and printer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process

Refactored Classes

class ReportDataFetcher {
    public String fetchData() {
        System.out.println("Fetching report data...");
        return "Raw Data from DB";
    }
}

class ReportFormatter {
    public String format(String rawData) {
        System.out.println("Formatting report...");
        return "--- Formatted Report ---
" + rawData.toUpperCase() + "
------------------------";
    }
}

class ReportPrinter {
    public void print(String formattedReport) {
        System.out.println("Printing report to console:
" + formattedReport);
    }
}

// Composition in main
ReportDataFetcher fetcher = new ReportDataFetcher();
ReportFormatter formatter = new ReportFormatter();
ReportPrinter printer = new ReportPrinter();

String rawData = fetcher.fetchData();
String formatted = formatter.format(rawData);
printer.print(formatted);
Benefits

Easier unit tests, clearer naming, and safe replacement of components later.

Refactor tip

Extract small classes and keep behavior identical before changing implementations.

Concrete example

If the app needs an email printer later, implement an EmailReportPrinter and pass it in; no existing code changes are required.

Key Takeaway

Extraction increases clarity and makes future change lower risk.

screens.title: Cohesion vs Coupling
screens.narratorSegment: Cohesion and coupling are practical lenses for judging your refactor. Cohesion measures how closely related the elements inside a module are; high cohesion means the class or component focuses on a single area of responsibility. Coupling measures dependency between modules; low coupling means changes in one module do not ripple to many others. SRP directly raises cohesion by grouping related methods and fields, and indirectly lowers coupling because collaborators communicate through small, well-defined interfaces. In practice look for indicators: many unrelated private methods or fields in one class suggest low cohesion. Frequent changes across modules together suggest high coupling. A common misconception is equating many classes with low coupling; you can have many classes that are tightly coupled if they share global state or call each other's internals. When refactoring, aim to replace internal knowledge with abstractions: tests should mock collaborators instead of setting up whole subsystems. For example, after splitting ReportGenerator, the formatter no longer depends on database details—its tests run with sample strings. Ask yourself when reading code: can I change this module without updating its collaborators' internals?

keyIdea.title: Cohesion & Coupling
keyIdea.text: High cohesion and low coupling are measurable outcomes of SRP-based refactoring and lead to easier maintenance and testing.

content.html:
Comparison

Cohesion vs Coupling

High Cohesion
  • Methods support the same responsibility.
  • Clear naming and focused tests.
  • Easy to replace implementations.
Low Coupling
  • Few assumptions about collaborators' internals.
  • Interfaces or abstractions isolate changes.
  • Integration points are explicit and testable.
Real check

If a single change requires edits in several modules, coupling is likely too high. Extract abstractions to reduce ripples.

Concrete example

Before and after SRP

Before: ReportGenerator mixes fetching, formatting, printing. Tests need DB and printer setups. After: Formatter tests use sample strings; fetcher tests stub the DB; printer tests use a fake output.
Key Takeaway

SRP-driven extraction increases cohesion and enables low-coupling architecture, which simplifies testing and extension.

screens.title: Refactoring Steps to Apply SRP
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring toward SRP is an incremental process you can use safely in production. Start by writing or running characterization tests that capture current behavior. Next, identify responsibility clusters inside the class: group methods and fields that change together or serve the same stakeholder. Create a small collaborator class for one cluster and delegate calls to it, keeping the original class behavior intact. Run tests to ensure nothing broke. Repeat extracting one responsibility at a time until the original class holds only its most central duty. A helpful rule is to extract things that vary independently: persistence, formatting, and notifications are classic candidates. After extraction, update tests to target collaborators directly and replace integration-heavy tests with focused unit tests backed by mocks or stubs. A common pitfall is extracting too eagerly without tests—this increases risk. Another pitfall is moving code without renaming; choose descriptive class names to make responsibilities explicit. This process preserves system behavior while improving structure and making future extensions safer. Which responsibility would you extract first in your current project? Refactoring Steps to Apply SRP means extract one responsibility at a time backed by tests; delegate until the original class is focused and collaborators are testable.. In practical terms, a repeatable process you can use in any refactor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor pattern
keyIdea.text: Extract one responsibility at a time backed by tests; delegate until the original class is focused and collaborators are testable.

content.html:
Process Flow

Step-by-step SRP refactor

1. Characterize

Write tests that capture current behavior to prevent regressions during refactor.

2. Identify

Group methods by reason to change. Map stakeholders and change drivers.

3. Extract

Create a new collaborator class and delegate responsibilities to it.

4. Verify

Run tests and adjust until behavior is unchanged. Convert integration tests to unit tests where possible.

5. Iterate

Repeat for other responsibilities until the class is focused and cohesive.

Concrete example

Start by extracting the persistence calls from Task into a TaskRepository, then extract notifications into TaskNotifier, keeping Task for domain logic.

Pitfall

Don't extract before you have tests: moving code without safety nets risks regressions and lost intent.

screens.title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
screens.narratorSegment: The Open/Closed Principle says software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. That sounds abstract, but it has a clear engineering goal: once you ship and test a component, adding new behavior should not require changing its existing source code. This reduces the risk of regressions and preserves tested code while allowing the system to grow. Achieving OCP commonly uses abstraction and polymorphism: define a stable interface or abstract type the client depends on, and add new implementations for new behaviors. For example, a discount calculation that uses an if-else on customer type violates OCP because adding a new type requires editing the calculator. The strategy pattern is a practical way to fix this: define a DiscountStrategy interface and implement concrete strategies for each customer type. The client depends on the interface and remains unchanged when new strategies are added. A misconception is treating enums and large switch statements as unavoidable; instead, recognize them as signals that an abstraction will simplify extension. Ask: what behavior might vary in the future and can be expressed behind a small interface?

keyIdea.title: OCP
keyIdea.text: Use interfaces and polymorphism so new behaviors can be added by creating new implementations instead of changing existing classes.

content.html:
Core Concept

Open/Closed Principle

Design so you can add new features without editing existing, tested code by programming to abstractions.

How to achieve it

Introduce interfaces or abstract classes and create new concrete implementations when behavior varies.

Misconception

OCP doesn't mean avoid all changes; it means avoid changing stable, tested clients when adding new variants of behavior.

Concrete example
// OCP Violation
class DiscountCalculator {
    public double calculateDiscount(String customerType, double amount) {
        if (customerType.equals("Regular")) {
            return amount * 0.05;
        } else if (customerType.equals("Premium")) {
            return amount * 0.10;
        }
        return 0;
    }
}
Why this is bad

Adding new customer types requires editing the calculator, risking regressions in tested logic.

screens.title: OCP Violation: DiscountCalculator
screens.narratorSegment: The DiscountCalculator example uses conditional logic to select discount rules based on a string customer type. It's easy to write, but every new customer category forces modification to the same method. That creates a maintenance hotspot: each edit must be tested and may accidentally change existing rules. Moreover, the logic is not easily reusable; you can't pass different strategies to other clients without duplicating the conditionals. A practical alternative is to make the behavior a separate strategy that adheres to a common interface. This design keeps the calculation client closed—its code doesn't change—and opens it for extension by creating a new strategy class. A subtle misconception is thinking that switch or if-else is acceptable because it's simple; simplicity for the moment can become technical debt when growth begins. As a concrete code observation, the violation often appears as repeated conditionals in many places—another sign to consolidate behavior behind an abstraction. In the next screen we'll show the interface-based refactor and how PriceCalculator becomes stable and easy to test. keyIdea.text: Conditionals on type signals an OCP violation; adding cases forces modification of existing, tested logic.

content.html:
Definition

Conditional-based OCP Violation

When behavior is chosen by type codes and conditionals, adding new variants requires editing the same code path.

Practical signposts
  • Large if-else or switch blocks around behavior selection.
  • Repeated case logic in multiple places.
  • Clients that need to change when a new variant is added.
Code Review
// Bad approach
class DiscountCalculator {
    public double calculateDiscount(String customerType, double amount) {
        if (customerType.equals("Regular")) {
            return amount * 0.05;
        } else if (customerType.equals("Premium")) {
            return amount * 0.10;
        } else if (customerType.equals("VIP")) {
            return amount * 0.15;
        }
        return 0;
    }
}
Pitfall

Editing this method to add a Newbie discount changes existing logic and requires re-testing the whole method.

screens.title: OCP Adherence: Strategy Pattern for Discounts
screens.narratorSegment: A straightforward fix to the conditional-based calculator is the strategy pattern. Define a DiscountStrategy interface with an applyDiscount method; implement concrete strategies for Regular, Premium, VIP, or Newbie customers. The PriceCalculator accepts a DiscountStrategy at construction and delegates the computation. This keeps PriceCalculator closed for modification: you can add new strategies without touching it. From a testing perspective, each strategy is small and easy to unit test; the calculator can be tested with a mock or a simple concrete strategy. A practical advantage is composition: different clients can use different strategies without duplicating logic. Beware of over-abstraction: introduce strategies only where behavior truly varies. In the example from the chapter, adding NewbieCustomerDiscount required only a new class, not edits to PriceCalculator. This pattern also supports runtime selection of strategies if needed, providing flexibility without sacrificing the stability of existing code. keyIdea.text: Introduce a small interface for varying behavior and implement each variant as a separate class so the client remains unchanged.

content.html:
Architecture

DiscountStrategy Example

interface DiscountStrategy {
    double applyDiscount(double amount);
}

class RegularCustomerDiscount implements DiscountStrategy {
    @Override
    public double applyDiscount(double amount) {
        return amount * 0.05;
    }
}

class VIPCustomerDiscount implements DiscountStrategy {
    @Override
    public double applyDiscount(double amount) {
        return amount * 0.15;
    }
}

class PriceCalculator {
    private DiscountStrategy discountStrategy;

    public PriceCalculator(DiscountStrategy strategy) {
        this.discountStrategy = strategy;
    }

    public double calculateFinalPrice(double basePrice) {
        return basePrice - discountStrategy.applyDiscount(basePrice);
    }
}
Concrete benefit

To add a new discount, implement DiscountStrategy and pass it into PriceCalculator. No edits to PriceCalculator are required.

Key Takeaway

Polymorphism lets you extend behavior safely; use it where behavior varies by type or policy.

keyIdea.title: Report strategy
keyIdea.text: Make the generator depend on a ReportStrategy so new report types are added via new classes without editing the generator.

content.html:
Process

ReportStrategy Example

interface ReportStrategy {
    String generate(java.util.List data);
}

class SimpleReportStrategy implements ReportStrategy {
    @Override
    public String generate(java.util.List data) {
        return "--- Simple Report ---
" + String.join("
", data) + "
--------------------";
    }
}

class NewReportGenerator {
    private ReportStrategy strategy;

    public NewReportGenerator(ReportStrategy strategy) {
        this.strategy = strategy;
    }

    public String generateReport(java.util.List data) {
        return strategy.generate(data);
    }
}
This design allows you to add CSV, JSON, or paginated reports by adding new classes that implement ReportStrategy, without changing NewReportGenerator.
Testing advantage

Test generator orchestration with a fake strategy. Test each strategy's formatting logic independently with sample data.

Key Takeaway

Dependency on an interface keeps the generator stable and makes adding report types low-risk.

screens.narratorSegment: This activity combines SRP and OCP in two small refactors. First, the Task refactor: start with a Task class that stores id, description, and status and currently contains commented persistence and notification methods. Run a simple main that creates a Task, saves it, and notifies; then change Task status and save again. content.html:
Application

Hands-on Activity

Follow these steps in your IDE or a simple Java file to practice refactoring safely.

SRP Refactor
  1. Identify persistence and notification code in Task and write characterization tests.
  2. Create TaskRepository.save(Task) and TaskNotifier.notify(Task).
  3. Delegate calls from application code and keep Task for domain rules.
  4. Run tests and replace integration checks with unit tests for collaborators.
Result

A focused Task class and two small, testable collaborators.

OCP Refactor
  1. Create ReportStrategy with generate(List<String> data).
  2. Implement SimpleReportStrategy and DetailedReportStrategy.
  3. Change ReportGenerator to accept a ReportStrategy in its constructor.
  4. Test adding a CSVReport without modifying the generator.
Result

A generator that is closed for modification and open to new report types via new strategy classes.

Why it matters

These refactors reduce regression risk, make tests smaller and faster, and let teams add features without changing core logic.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these concise concepts front of mind as you design and refactor: SRP asks that a class have only one reason to change, which you can check by mapping stakeholders and change drivers. OCP asks that systems be open to extension but closed to modification; achieve this by programming to an abstraction and adding new implementations for new behavior. Cohesion increases when responsibilities are grouped sensibly, and coupling decreases when modules depend on small, stable interfaces. Use the strategy pattern and small collaborator classes to convert conditional logic and mixed responsibilities into extensible and testable designs. Common mistakes to avoid include premature abstraction, extracting without tests, and confusing many classes with good design. Instead, extract when behavior varies or when clear separate reasons to change appear. These principles guide daily decisions: break responsibilities when changes would affect different stakeholders, and design extension points when behavior may grow. fullNarratorScript:
As your projects grow, fragile classes and rigid conditionals become the main source of bugs and slow change. In this lesson we concentrate on two SOLID rules that help avoid that: Single Responsibility, which keeps classes focused on one reason to change, and Open/Closed, which enables adding features without altering tested code. You will see concrete Java examples that first demonstrate common violations and then show how to refactor them into clearer, testable components. For SRP we use a ReportGenerator that mixes data access, formatting, and output; for OCP we use a discount calculator that uses conditional logic instead of polymorphism. Each example highlights why cohesion and low coupling matter for testing, team work, and incremental extension. By the end you will be able to spot responsibilities that should be separated, design small interfaces, and choose strategy-style abstractions to add new behavior safely. Think about the last time you changed a class and unintentionally broke a feature — this chapter gives you patterns to prevent that. Ready to learn how to turn a Swiss army knife class into a set of precise tools?

By the end of this chapter you will master focused design and safe extension patterns. First, you will understand why design principles reduce maintenance cost and improve testability, and be able to explain how SRP and OCP contribute to that goal. Second, you will identify Single Responsibility Principle violations: you'll recognize classes that mix unrelated behaviors and explain how separate stakeholders or change reasons reveal those violations. Third, you will apply SRP by refactoring classes such as a ReportGenerator into distinct components for fetching, formatting, and output, improving cohesion and lowering coupling. Fourth, you will explain and apply the Open/Closed Principle using abstraction and polymorphism, for example turning a conditional-based discount calculator into a strategy-based design that accepts new customer types without modifying existing code. Each objective maps to hands-on changes: refactoring Task persistence and notifications, and creating report strategies. These skills matter because they let you extend systems incrementally, avoid regressions, and work in teams without breaking unrelated features. Will you be able to spot the single reason to change when you look at a class? That's the question you'll practice answering.

This chapter pairs explanation with practical refactoring. You will refactor a Task class that currently mixes persistence, notification, and business state into separate collaborators. That exercise gives you concrete practice applying SRP: move save operations to a TaskRepository and notifications to a TaskNotifier while keeping Task responsible for its own business rules. The assessment follows with a report generator refactor to a ReportStrategy interface and two concrete implementations. You will prove OCP competency by adding a new report type without changing the existing generator. These activities emphasize safe, incremental change: you validate behavior at each step, keep tests around unchanged classes, and introduce abstractions only where behavior varies. A common misconception is that abstraction always costs simplicity; we will contrast when a small interface reduces overall complexity and when it is premature. By practicing both SRP and OCP you learn a rhythm: identify responsibility boundaries, extract small classes, and introduce interfaces for variation points. That rhythm is the most reliable way to keep code healthy as systems grow.

Single Responsibility means a class should have one primary reason to change. Practically, that means its responsibilities should be cohesive: methods and fields should support a single domain of concern. A reason to change is often tied to a stakeholder or a feature area. For example, database schema changes are one reason, formatting requirements another, and notification delivery a third. When these concerns live inside the same class, a small change in one area can break unrelated behavior, and tests become brittle. High cohesion and low coupling are the desired outcomes: cohesion groups related behavior, while low coupling reduces ripple effects between modules. A common mistake is thinking SRP requires a class with only one method; the goal is meaningful grouping, not tiny classes for their own sake. To evaluate a class, ask: who would request a change here? If different teams or features would make separate requests, you likely have an SRP violation. As a concrete example, the ReportGenerator that fetches data, formats it, and prints it mixes three reasons to change. Refactoring splits those into a fetcher, a formatter, and a printer, which improves testability and lets each piece evolve independently. Consider: what single responsibility would you give your next class?

Let's walk through the ReportGenerator example to understand exactly why it violates SRP. The class contains methods to fetch data, format it, and print it. Each method corresponds to a different reason to change: if the data source changes, you modify fetching; if the layout or header requirements change, you modify formatting; if output moves to email or file, you alter printing. Mixing these in one class creates high coupling: tests for the formatter may need database setup, and a change to printing could break report content. A concrete run shown in the code prints messages for each step, which is useful for demonstration but not for production. A common misconception is to treat logging or convenience printing as harmless responsibilities — in practice they create hidden dependencies and make code harder to reuse. When you refactor, you extract responsibilities into classes such as ReportDataFetcher, ReportFormatter, and ReportPrinter, each replaceable or mockable in isolation. In the next screen we'll show the refactored version with small, testable classes and describe how cohesion improves and coupling decreases. Ask yourself: which collaborator would you mock in a unit test for formatting?

Refactoring to respect SRP means extracting collaborators with clear roles. In the example refactor we create ReportDataFetcher to handle data retrieval, ReportFormatter to prepare the presentation, and ReportPrinter to handle output. Each class exposes a small A P I: fetch returns raw data, format produces a textual report, and print sends the report to a destination. That separation allows focused unit tests: you can test formatting with mocked raw data, test printing with a fake output sink, and test fetching with an isolated data source or stub. The refactored main function composes these collaborators and performs the workflow. This approach raises cohesion inside each component and lowers coupling between them. A misconception is that this adds too many classes; however, these smaller classes are simpler to reason about, easier to name, and tend to have fewer dependencies. When you refactor, keep behavior unchanged initially and run simple console checks. Later you can replace implementations—swap a console printer for an email sender—without touching the formatter. As you practice, ask: which tests become isolated after extraction, and which integration tests remain? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cohesion and coupling are practical lenses for judging your refactor. Cohesion measures how closely related the elements inside a module are; high cohesion means the class or component focuses on a single area of responsibility. Coupling measures dependency between modules; low coupling means changes in one module do not ripple to many others. SRP directly raises cohesion by grouping related methods and fields, and indirectly lowers coupling because collaborators communicate through small, well-defined interfaces. In practice look for indicators: many unrelated private methods or fields in one class suggest low cohesion. Frequent changes across modules together suggest high coupling. A common misconception is equating many classes with low coupling; you can have many classes that are tightly coupled if they share global state or call each other's internals. When refactoring, aim to replace internal knowledge with abstractions: tests should mock collaborators instead of setting up whole subsystems. For example, after splitting ReportGenerator, the formatter no longer depends on database details—its tests run with sample strings. Ask yourself when reading code: can I change this module without updating its collaborators' internals?

A common pitfall is extracting too eagerly without tests—this increases risk. Another pitfall is moving code without renaming; choose descriptive class names to make responsibilities explicit. This process preserves system behavior while improving structure and making future extensions safer. Which responsibility would you extract first in your current project? This activity combines SRP and OCP in two small refactors. First, the Task refactor: start with a Task class that stores id, description, and status and currently contains commented persistence and notification methods. Modify the generator to accept a ReportStrategy in its constructor and call generate on it. Create a small list of strings as report data and run both generators. Keep these concise concepts front of mind as you design and refactor: SRP asks that a class have only one reason to change, which you can check by mapping stakeholders and change drivers. OCP asks that systems be open to extension but closed to modification; achieve this by programming to an abstraction and adding new implementations for new behavior. Cohesion increases when responsibilities are grouped sensibly, and coupling decreases when modules depend on small, stable interfaces. Use the strategy pattern and small collaborator classes to convert conditional logic and mixed responsibilities into extensible and testable designs. Common mistakes to avoid include premature abstraction, extracting without tests, and confusing many classes with good design. Instead, extract when behavior varies or when clear separate reasons to change appear. These principles guide daily decisions: break responsibilities when changes would affect different stakeholders, and design extension points when behavior may grow. Keep three short reminders on your desk: first, ask who would request a change to a class — if the answer lists different stakeholders, consider splitting responsibilities. Second, when you see conditionals selecting behavior across types, consider introducing an interface and concrete implementations so clients remain unchanged when variants are added. Third, always test before and after refactor: characterization tests make safe extraction possible and keep behavior stable. These heuristics help you make small, safe decisions: extract one responsibility at a time, use clear names for collaborators, and favor narrow interfaces for points of variation. Over time this habit reduces regression risk and makes teams more productive because individual code areas become easier to understand and evolve.
